extracted.intended_audience: British educated public and policymakers (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and arguing constitutional principles of sovereignty, succession, and the proper limits of revolutionary change in Britain, with historical statutory examples (Declaration of Right, acts of William and Mary, 12th & 13th of William).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to choose our own governors
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed by some as a fundamental right of the people: 'To choose our own governors.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats this as a 'new, and hitherto unheard-of bill of rights' claimed by a faction but asserts it is fictitious: the Declaration of Right and subsequent statutes contain no suggestion of a general right to elect the sovereign; historic practice and statute instead bind the nation to hereditary succession. If such a right had existed previously, the Revolution acts effectively renounced it for posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to cashier governors for misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed right: 'To cashier them for misconduct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page rejects a loose notion of 'misconduct' as a sufficient ground. At the Revolution ministers and crown were only removed/held to account where there was 'a design, continued by a multitude of illegal overt acts, to subvert the Protestant church and state, and their fundamental...laws and liberties'—i.e. more than mere misconduct. Practical safeguards preferred are frequent parliamentary inspection, impeachment, and statutory rules (e.g., that a pardon under the great seal is not pleadable to impeachment) rather than carte blanche popular cashiering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to frame a government for ourselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed right: 'To frame a government for ourselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats this as part of the same trio of fictitious rights attributed to the Revolution Society and argues that the relevant constitutional statutes (Declaration of Right, acts of William & Mary) do not grant a general right for the people to reframe government at will; changes were made by legislature within the existing constitutional framework, not by establishing a perpetual elective principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of Right as corner-stone tying rights and succession
rubrics_metrics.description: The Declaration of Right (1 William & Mary, sess. ii. ch. 2) is described as 'the corner-stone of our constitution' where 'these rights and this succession are declared in one body, and bound indissolubly together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Declaration of Right as primary constitutional text: its deliberate omission of any general elective right and its explicit coupling of 'rights and the succession of the crown' indicate that liberty was secured by institutional arrangements that include hereditary succession. Interpretations of the Revolution should be grounded in that statute, not in later abstract theories of popular election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession and certainty of title
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereditary succession (by common law and statute) is the established rule: succession should be certain to preserve 'the unity, peace, and tranquillity of this nation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative measures (e.g., later Limitation acts, 12th & 13th William) deliberately fuse an hereditary crown with hereditary allegiance to prevent doubtful titles that would 'but too much resemble an election.' Deviations from hereditary order are allowed only as narrow, exceptional devices to meet necessity and should not be turned into general rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on the moral competence of sovereign institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although parliament exercises wide (abstract) competence, it is not morally competent to dissolve essential institutions or to renounce core constitutional engagements—the constituent parts of the state must 'hold their public faith with each other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: special-case laws or acts of necessity should not be generalized into immutable principles. Bodies such as the House of Lords or Commons cannot morally abdicate their role; the constitution imposes obligations preventing wholesale surrender of the public trust. Changes must respect the obligations and continuity of the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occasional deviation confined to remedy of specific defect (conservation and correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A state must have means of change to conserve itself, but changes at times of emergency should be confined 'to the peccant part only' and effected without decomposing the whole civil and political mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the legislature departs from strict hereditary order for necessity, it should preserve the underlying principle and adapt only what is defective; reforms should regenerate deficient parts through the unchanged parts of the constitution rather than creating a wholly new civil order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical consequences of making election the sole lawful title
rubrics_metrics.description: If election were treated as the only lawful title to the throne, earlier sovereigns and the statutes passed under them would be put in question—'no one act of the princes who preceded this era of fictitious election can be valid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain legal continuity: constitutional legitimacy depends on continuity of titles and statutes. Avoid doctrines that would retroactively invalidate past authority, as that would destabilize laws and institutions (habeas corpus, petition of right, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministerial responsibility and parliamentary safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Revolution constitutional design emphasized ministerial responsibility—ministers 'should serve the crown on the terms of that declaration'—and parliamentary oversight (frequent meetings, impeachment) as the proper security against maladministration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer structural, institutional checks (frequent parliaments, impeachment procedures, statutory limits on pardon pleas) to populist remedies like arbitrary removal of rulers. These statutory and procedural mechanisms are presented as effective means to secure liberty without undermining constitutional stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for virtual abdication or forfeiture of the crown
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolution-era declaration charged King James II with having 'endeavoured to subvert the constitution... having violated the fundamental laws, and having withdrawn himself out of the kingdom, hath abdicated the government, and the throne is thereby vacant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete wrongdoing—a sustained design and illegal overt acts to subvert constitution and church/state—as the standard for treating a sovereign as having vacated the throne. This is a much stricter standard than vague 'misconduct' and provides legal language for justifying extreme remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative limitation of succession to secure religion and continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament's limitation of the crown (e.g., naming Princess Sophia and limiting succession to Protestant heirs) aimed to connect the new line with the old stock and secure 'an inheritable line... connected with the old stock of inheritance in King James the First.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislature may lawfully shape succession rules (religious tests, dynastic selections) to protect what it views as essential for the nation's stability and liberties; such statutory limitations are instruments to preserve unity and the 'healthy habit' of hereditary succession despite foreign or inconvenient contingencies.
